claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires preparation above 2300 °C.
Conventional high-temperature preparation of ZrB2 produces coarse grains.
Conventional high-temperature preparation increases the propensity for residual porosity in ZrB2.
A liquid-phase precursor method can produce nanosized, homogeneous diboride powder.
The cited liquid-phase method produced ultrafine single-phase high-entropy diboride powders at 1800 °C.
The cited high-entropy diboride powders had average grain sizes of 340–570 nm.
A liquid-phase precursor route can produce nanosized, homogeneous powder specifically for pure single-phase ZrB2.
Spark plasma sintering can consolidate precursor-derived pure ZrB2 at approximately 1800–2000 °C.
Nanostructuring increases powder surface area and sintering activity.
The precursor-derived powder enhances mass transport and densification kinetics during spark plasma sintering.
Lower sintering temperatures minimize grain growth in ZrB2.
Lower sintering temperatures limit void generation in ZrB2.
The combined precursor and rapid-sintering process yields dense, pore-free single-phase ZrB2.
The modified process lowers the ZrB2 sintering temperature by several hundred degrees relative to conventional preparation.
Reduced residual porosity improves the mechanical strength and structural integrity of ZrB2.
Reduced porosity decreases liquid infiltration into ZrB2 during plating-bath exposure.
Precursor-derived ZrB2 will form fewer holes and retain greater mechanical integrity during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The precursor process requires an inert or reducing atmosphere.
The cited liquid-phase method is not applicable to all high-entropy ceramic powders and is unfavorable for single-phase borides when the size-difference factor exceeds 3.9%.
Direct experimental evidence for applying this precursor-plus-SPS process to pure single-phase ZrB2 is limited.
